newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.S.'s Cohen expected to discuss arms sales in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: U.S.'s Cohen expected to discuss arms sales in Gulf.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen is expected to deliver a familiar message on his first Gulf tour -- America will protect its allies from Iran and Iraq and offers the best high-tech weapons money can buy.
"Cohen will be waving the American security and commercial flag," said a Western diplomat in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
"He will be reiterating that the U.S. is still standing firm against Iraq and Iran and he will discuss potential sales of U.S. fighter planes to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates," he said.
Cohen is due in Saudi Arabia on Saturday and then heads to Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE and Oman before returning to Washington on Wednesday.

It will be his first visit as defence secretary to the strategically important and oil-rich Gulf, where the United States maintains a major naval presence as well as warplanes that keep watch over southern Iraq.
The United States has vowed to protect its Gulf Arab allies from any security threats from Iran or Iraq.

U.S. defence officials have called the Gulf trip a get-acquainted visit and said they did not expect any final report from Saudi Arabia on a bombing that killed 19 American airmen in eastern Saudi Arabia last June.
A U.S. statement said force protection would be one of the key issues that Cohen would discuss on the trip in light of the bombing in Saudi Arabia.
Western diplomats and defence industry executives expect Cohen to lobby for U.S. firms seeking arms sales to Gulf Arab states with large appetites for sophisticated hardware.
"He will be advocating American defence firms very strongly," said a U.S. defence executive based in Abu Dhabi.
The United States has said key ally Saudi Arabia was shopping for fighters, but reacted cautiously to a report it would buy up to 100 Lockheed Martin Corp F-16s in a multi-billion dollar deal.

Talk of a potential purchase raised Israeli concerns and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said a deal would violate the strategic balance in the Middle East -- the type of talk that irritates Arab states.

"This issue is on the back burner. The Saudis don't like Israel having veto power over their arms purchases and they can simply go elsewhere for planes. This is their card," said a Western diplomat in Riyadh.
"Cohen is expected to try to ease any Saudi anger over Israel's reaction."
A defence industry executive said Lockheed was preparing a package that included prices and details on a potential training programme in an effort to clinch a fighter deal with the Saudis.
"I don't expect a deal in 1997 because of financing," he said. "It is always difficult to tell if the Saudis are comfortable enough financially to make a big purchase."

Cohen will also be pushing for Lockheed in Abu Dhabi where it is in a fierce race with France's Dassault Aviation to sell the oil-rich emirate up to 80 advanced combat planes in a deal potentially worth $6 billion.
Also competing for the sale is the Eurofighter 2000, made by a consortium of British Aerospace, Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA), Spain's CASA and Italy's Alenia Spa.
An American industry official said Lockheed had recently made gains in talks with UAE air force officials but stressed that the French have been lobbying hard.
"There has been much progress in recent discussions," he said.
